content: Cefdinir, like other cephalosporins, exerts its bactericidal activity by inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis. It is stable in the presence of certain β-lactamase enzymes, but not all. Consequently, many organisms that are resistant to penicillins and some cephalosporins remain susceptible to cefdinir. Cefdinir has demonstrated activity against most strains of specific microorganisms in both in vitro studies and clinical infections, as outlined in the Indications and Usage section. Aerobic Gram-Positive Microorganisms Staphylococcus aureus (including strains that produce β-lactamase enzymes) Streptococcus pneumoniae (penicillin-susceptible strains only) Streptococcus pyogenes Note: Cefdinir is not effective against methicillin-resistant staphylococci. Aerobic Gram-Negative Microorganisms Haemophilus influenzae (including β-lactamase-producing strains) Haemophilus parainfluenzae (including β-lactamase-producing strains) Moraxella catarrhalis (including β-lactamase-producing strains) Cefdinir has shown in vitro minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of ≤1 mcg/mL against ≥90% of strains of certain microorganisms. However, the clinical significance of these findings is unknown, as the safety and efficacy of cefdinir in treating infections caused by these microorganisms have not been established in well-controlled clinical trials. Additional Aerobic Gram-Positive Microorganisms Staphylococcus epidermidis (methicillin-susceptible strains only) Streptococcus agalactiae Viridans group streptococci Note: Cefdinir is inactive against Enterococcus species and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus species. Additional Aerobic Gram-Negative Microorganisms Citrobacter diversus Escherichia coli Klebsiella pneumoniae Proteus mirabilis Note: Cefdinir is not effective against Pseudomonas or Enterobacter species. Susceptibility Testing Quantitative methods, such as dilution techniques, are used to determine the MICs of cefdinir, which estimate the susceptibility of bacteria to the antimicrobial compound. These tests should follow standardized procedures, including the use of standardized inoculum concentrations and cefdinir powder concentrations. MIC values should be interpreted based on established criteria. For Streptococcus spp., isolates with MICs ≤0.06 mcg/mL (for S. pneumoniae) or ≤0.12 mcg/mL (for other streptococci) are considered susceptible to cefdinir. Testing cefdinir against penicillin-intermediate or penicillin-resistant isolates is not recommended due to the lack of reliable interpretive criteria. A Susceptible report indicates that the pathogen is likely to be inhibited if the antimicrobial compound in the blood reaches usual achievable concentrations. An Intermediate report suggests equivocal results, and the test should be repeated if alternative drugs are not feasible. This category may have clinical applicability in body sites where the drug is physiologically concentrated or when high dosages can be used. It also provides a buffer zone to account for minor technical variations in testing. A Resistant report indicates that the pathogen is unlikely to be inhibited at usual blood concentrations, and alternative therapy should be selected. Standardized susceptibility testing requires the use of laboratory control microorganisms to ensure the technical accuracy of procedures. Standard cefdinir powder should yield specific MIC values. Diffusion Techniques Quantitative methods involving zone diameter measurements also provide reproducible estimates of bacterial susceptibility to cefdinir. A standardized procedure uses paper disks impregnated with 5 mcg of cefdinir to test susceptibility. Results from single-disk susceptibility tests should be interpreted based on established criteria. For Streptococcus spp., isolates of S. pneumoniae should be tested with a 1 mcg oxacillin disk. Isolates with oxacillin zone sizes ≥20 mm are susceptible to penicillin and can be considered susceptible to cefdinir. Streptococci other than S. pneumoniae should be tested with a 10-unit penicillin disk. Isolates with penicillin zone sizes ≥28 mm are susceptible to penicillin and can be considered susceptible to cefdinir. As with dilution techniques, diffusion methods require the use of laboratory control microorganisms to ensure the technical accuracy of procedures.
